# Senior layer: fiction

Use for a big job, a senior review, or when the user asks for senior-level work. It adds to SKILL.md. Fiction sourcing is thin: most rules here are workshop practice, not measured findings, and are tagged that way. `[verified: URL]` means the page was opened (some pages quote the books, which were not opened); `[practice]` means common craft advice with no opened source.

## Psychic distance

- **Treat distance as a dial and set it on purpose.** It is the distance the reader feels between themselves and the events. Far: "It was winter of the year 1853. A large man stepped out of a doorway." Close: "God how he hated these damn snowstorms." Check: the distance in the opening matches what the scene needs. [verified: https://www.eckleburg.org/psychic-distance/]
- **Do not shift distance without a reason.** Sudden shifts inside a paragraph read as careless. Check: no unmotivated drop from "Mary Borden hated woodpeckers" to "Lord, she thought" to "The young woman". [verified: https://www.eckleburg.org/psychic-distance/]
- **Practise by rewriting one paragraph at two distances.** Check: both versions are shown and the better one chosen. [verified: https://teachingwriting.stanford.edu/psychic-distance]
- **Move in for high intensity, draw back for transitions.** Check: the closest passage is the climax, not the setup. [verified: https://www.eckleburg.org/psychic-distance/]

## Scene function

- **Every scene needs a goal, opposition and a change.** A scene has a goal, conflict and disaster; a sequel has reaction, dilemma and decision. A unit with neither is filler. Check: say the goal, who blocks it and what is different at the end, or mark it a sequel with a decision. [verified: https://writershelpingwriters.net/2015/01/writing-patterns-fiction-scene-sequel/]
- **Summarise routine, dramatise choice.** Check: time that passes without a decision is one line. [practice]
- **Cut or merge a unit that changes nothing.** Check: removing it leaves the next scene still working. [practice]

## Want and need

- **Give each lead a want (what they chase) and a need (what they lack), often opposed.** The tension sits in the gap. Check: you can write both in one sentence each, and they differ. [practice]
- **Let the want cost the need.** Check: the ending shows what the pursuit lost. [practice]

## Subtext

- **Let people talk about the thing next to the thing.** Stated feelings flatten a scene. Check: at least one spoken line differs from what the speaker wants. "'Nice tie. New?' She straightened his collar and didn't look up." beats "I'm angry you forgot." [practice]
- **Do not follow a dodge with the real feeling.** Check: no line explains the one before it. [practice]

## Revision passes

- **Revise in separate passes, one variable each.** Polishing everything at once hides the real problem. Check: you can name the pass you are in. [practice]
  1. Structure: move, cut, merge scenes.
  2. Want and cost per scene.
  3. Dialogue and subtext.
  4. Distance and point of view.
  5. Sentence rhythm and specifics.
  6. Cut about a tenth.
  7. Proof.
- **Run the tells scan last, not first.** Names and phrases are cheap to fix; shape is not. Check: `references/tells.md` is read after pass 5. [practice]

## Build on

No strong fiction skill is installed, so this is original work. For dialogue and distance, `references/craft.md` in this skill already applies. For NPC or quest text inside a UI, `ux-copy` (design plugin) gives short, clear wording; if it is missing, keep lines short and in character. Link only; no licence found.
